
- A writer creates both trees under one private staging root. Extract, compile, analyze, runtime-state capture and web-clone context materialization may write only there.
- Before publication, one strict root manifest binds task, source/final URL, viewport, action digest, both complete file inventories, the source-package manifest SHA and every copied raw-to-projection file by path, bytes and SHA-256.
- The complete staging directory is renamed once to its unique immutable snapshot directory. Published snapshot files are never modified.
- `fd/source-snapshot.json` is the only current identity authority and has strict shape `{ version, taskID, snapshotID, manifestSha256 }`. It is replaced by one atomic temporary-file rename only after the immutable directory and every hash validate.
- Every reader resolves the pointer once to a frozen handle and uses only that handle for the whole operation. It never rereads current midway. Persisted Browser Preview evidence stores its exact snapshot ID, manifest SHA and source artifact SHA, so historical evidence resolves its pinned snapshot rather than the current pointer.
- Runtime-state recapture pins one explicit parent snapshot, copies the parent's raw evidence into a new private staging root, performs the expert-declared complete action protocol, regenerates the source package, validates and publishes a new snapshot. Any action, capture, copy, manifest, cancellation or pointer failure leaves the old pointer and old bytes unchanged.
- Concurrent publication is optimistic and exact: a writer supplies `expectedParentSnapshotID` and publication rejects parent drift. There is no last-writer-wins merge, retry fallback, fixed-directory alias, symlink/junction or read-side repair.

The existing `Filesystem.writeAtomic` pattern may be reused for the small pointer after its temporary name is made unique and Windows replacement behavior is executable-tested. The content-addressed `write wx -> rename -> verify` pattern in `expert-squad/package-tool-bundle.ts` may be adapted without importing that package concern. The in-process `util/lock.ts`, package-manager backup swap, SDK mirror transaction and sidecar PID cleanup are not publication authorities for this snapshot.

#### Confirmed DOM identity defect

Independent executable counterexamples prove four current false greens: production `BrowserPreviewRuntimeEvidence` accepts a declared `unrelated-control` locator while actual target, subject and focus claim Block Monitor; the complete browser report accepts an unrelated source action target; it accepts the same target locator drift; and it accepts a different active element when the short selector is reused. The capture path actually resolves real nodes, but the persisted schema discards that node identity and later validators compare only a truncated selector or Block Monitor text.

The replacement is one capture-scope DOM identity protocol:

```ts
type ResolvedElement<L, E> = {
  locator: L
  nodeID: string
  element: E
}
```

- A page/context-local `WeakMap<Element, nodeID>` assigns one stable node ID per real DOM node. The same node keeps its ID across action, subject and focus inspection; two nodes remain different even when tag, classes, short selector, text or geometry collide.
- Source action target and visible postcondition carry their exact resolved locator, node ID and element. Snapshot focus carries the same capture-scope node ID. Production Zod parses Node sidecar results before any file is written; the tool imports the same requested-action schema instead of defining a parallel input grammar.
- Target action and comparison subject each carry their own exact resolved locator/node. Platform schema proves declared locator equals resolved locator and verifies each resolved record; it does not require every action target to equal the comparison subject because a general interaction may click a control and compare a panel.
- The frontend-replica E2E policy, not the platform schema, requires Block Monitor after/keyboard evidence to bind action target, comparison subject and active element to the same node ID. Its source state-preparation action must bind declared locator -> actual target -> initial focused node, while the visible expectation binds its own declared locator -> observed node.
- Selector, label, text, geometry and `subjectFocused` remain diagnostics/facts, never identity. No selector candidates, name guessing, site-specific core rule or fallback is introduced.

DOM call points are source capture/schema/tool, target region schema/capture/runtime schema, comparison/persistence/routes, browser collection/final schema/declaration, supervisor revalidation and parent handoff. The benchmark verifier remains an independent consumer, but production input/capture semantics have one Zod source.

#### 2026-07-13 SourceSnapshotStore codex review feedback

The first `SourceSnapshotStore` implementation and its five focused tests were independently reviewed against frozen blobs and returned `REJECT`. The reviewer executed counterexamples rather than relying on source inspection. The following defects are part of the active acceptance contract and must not be silently removed from later summaries:

1. A projected package file can be relabeled `generated`, allowing its bytes to diverge from the raw counterpart while the aggregate still publishes. The replacement must define one exact generated-file set; every other projected file is an exact raw copy, and capture reference, package provenance reference and root copy records must agree.
2. Required projected artifacts and entrypoints can be deleted from both manifest arrays and still publish. One exported required-artifact contract must be validated as an exact set rather than accepting any nonempty declaration.
3. `createChildStaging` trusts an in-memory handle and copies a parent whose immutable bytes may have been damaged after resolution. It must revalidate the complete pinned parent before copy and compare the copied raw inventory with the frozen parent manifest before returning staging.
4. Persistent publication claim files became a second current authority and can deadlock all future writers after process exit. Publication must use an operating-system-released cross-process lock, reread the complete pointer identity inside the lock, and leave no durable claim authority.
5. A `source-snapshots` junction can redirect immutable publication outside the task runtime. Every existing ancestor and publication destination must be verified against the task root through real paths; nested links and externally mutable linked files are forbidden.
6. Publication compares only the parent snapshot ID, so a pointer with the wrong task or manifest SHA is silently repaired. A malformed or drifted pointer must fail without modification; comparison covers version, task, snapshot and manifest SHA.
7. Required IR reads use an optional JSON helper that swallows read and parse failures. Required artifacts use strict production schemas; an optional artifact may be absent, but if present and malformed it also fails.

The new executable matrix includes cross-process same-parent contention, owner termination and subsequent recovery, cancellation and injected pointer/rename faults, old-pointer/old-byte preservation, no staging/lock/temp/orphan residue, parent corruption before and during copy, full pointer drift, required projected-file deletion, illegal `generated` relabeling for reference and interaction artifacts, junction/symlink and external-link mutation, malformed required IR/audit JSON, and independent raw/projected/package-manifest/root-manifest mutations. #### 2026-07-14 publication authority and producer terminal-semantics Recall

The latest exact-tree independent review returned `REJECT`; no Store or producer acceptance from an earlier blob applies to the current tree. The reviewed blobs were `source-snapshot-store.ts` `357c2ce46638e483453f89650a62b21738f850da`, `webpage-evidence.ts` `21e8261f2df3824cc7188223d374bc5e0db3095b`, `source-snapshot-store.test.ts` `1dd9ef130b83a77113bdbd8f79e89a3a8f04e7f3`, `source-snapshot-publisher-child.ts` `5afc9bb24db26c76e8d34edc6582653bd4ea3e9c` and `webpage-evidence.test.ts` `b88e35396aa197e273650885061cc1e860fc0a7c`. The reviewer confirmed pointer close/removal aggregation, final-directory and pointer-rename rollback, explicit committed lock-cleanup outcome and real-process initial-parent exclusion, but found five remaining defects:

1. The project-local `source-snapshot.lock` is a replaceable pathname. Its file lock binds the opened filesystem object, so unlinking or replacing the pathname after the last pre-operation inode check lets another publisher lock the replacement and enter the same logical critical section.
2. Producer progress delivery can throw after the current pointer was committed, making a successful publication reject. The post-publication artifact read/revalidation has the same false-failure shape.
3. A failing `failed` progress callback replaces the original stage failure instead of retaining both errors.
4. The producer emits `publish:completed` before a second `publish:committed_with_cleanup_failure` terminal-like event, and the latter has no executable test.
5. `publicationLockCleanup.errors` remains mutable even though the containing object is frozen.

The whole-repository call-point scan found one production publication-lock implementation, two runtime-path fields, one direct lock-carrier negative test, two cross-process publisher tests, producer progress consumers in Research, and producer progress assertions in Orchestrator and Research tests. `fs-native-extensions` is also referenced by the native packaging scripts and build-artifact tests. No second production SourceSnapshot mutex implementation exists. Progress callbacks are externally observable side effects and therefore cannot be silently swallowed, but a callback is not allowed to retroactively change an already committed current pointer into a failed publication result.

The correction design removes the project-local lock pathname rather than adding another inode check. Publication will lock a deterministic non-SQLite byte range on the already-open OpenCorvus database file, which is the existing process-wide runtime authority named by the project authority marker. The lock stores no owner, claim, current identity or recovery record; it is released by the operating system when the descriptor or process closes. The project and task identity select the byte range, so identical publications contend while a hash collision only serializes unrelated publications. Replacing the opened database file is an existing database-authority integrity failure, not a SourceSnapshot alternate-lock path. The implementation must still verify the opened descriptor/path identity before and after acquisition, use the complete SourceSnapshot parent identity under the lock, remove both obsolete runtime-path lock fields, and prove cross-process contention and owner termination recovery. This design is pending implementation and independent review; it is not accepted by this record.

The producer correction will construct the strict published binding before pointer replacement, emit exactly one terminal publish status, and return an explicit committed diagnostic if post-commit progress delivery or lock cleanup fails. Pre-commit operation failures remain failures; if failure-progress delivery also fails, the thrown `AggregateError` retains the original stage error first. No post-commit artifact read, schema reconstruction or progress exception may reject the committed result. Tests must inject completed-progress, failed-progress and lock-cleanup failures and assert exact pointer/result/error semantics. The diagnostic and its nested error arrays must be deeply immutable. This design is likewise pending implementation and independent review.

#### 2026-07-14 database byte-range publication authority codex rejection

Independent review of the replacement database-file byte-range lock found executable cross-platform and authority failures, so the preceding byte-range design is rejected rather than accepted or retained as an alternate path:

1. `fs-native-extensions` requests a write lock for the range. A database descriptor opened read-only fails with `EBADF` on Linux, while the macOS implementation rejects nonzero offset or length with `EINVAL`. OpenCorvus supports both platforms, so the proposed primitive is not a portable publication authority.
2. `Database.OpenedPath()` alone does not prove that the current database owns the worktree. Two processes using different `OPENCORVUS_HOME` values open different database files and can both acquire the same logical project/task range; an executable initial-publication counterexample produced two fulfilled publishers.
3. Replacing the database path through `Database.resetFiles` while the old descriptor remains locked allows the replacement database file to acquire the same range concurrently. Path/descriptor inode checks cannot repair an operation-window replacement race.
4. `runLiveWebpageEvidenceStage` returned the asynchronous publish helper without awaiting it. A throwing `publish:started` progress callback therefore bypassed the outer cleanup catch and left the private SourceSnapshot staging directory behind.

The complete call-point scan for this correction covers the sole production `withPublicationLock`, exported `SourceSnapshotPublicationLock`, the Store producer, the lock-holder and publisher child fixtures, Store cleanup injection, producer progress tests, all `ProjectRuntimeAuthority.open/require/remove/relocateToGit/hasNonGitAuthority` consumers, and the `DatabaseIdentity.currentUUID` implementation. No second production SourceSnapshot mutex is present.

The next candidate design is one short-lived SQLite `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction on a dedicated connection to the database named by a strict worktree runtime authority. Acquisition is retried only for the structured `SQLITE_BUSY` result and remains abortable; no database row, owner claim, lease, stale timeout or repair path is created. After acquisition, the dedicated connection must read the persisted database UUID and match the project authority before any filesystem publication step. This closes the different-home and database-replacement counterexamples even when a stale pre-acquisition authority value was read. The transaction performs no product-data write and is rolled back solely to release the cross-process lock after pointer publication. Operation failure remains pre-commit failure; rollback/close failure after a successful pointer replacement is an explicit committed cleanup diagnostic. Because SQLite serializes writers at database scope, the implementation and review must measure and document that bottleneck; it may be accepted only if the filesystem critical section remains limited to final validation, immutable rename and pointer replacement.

The producer must also `await` the publish helper inside its stage wrapper so pre-publication progress failure reaches the existing staging cleanup path. Tests must reproduce a throwing `publish:started` callback and assert no staging, immutable, pointer-temp or current-pointer residue. The SQLite design and producer fix remain pending executable tests and a new exact-tree independent review; neither is accepted by this record.

Codex review then rejected the SQLite candidate as the final platform abstraction because `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` is a database-wide writer mutex. The required parent/staging/final inventory and hash verification can take hundreds of milliseconds or seconds, so that mutex would block unrelated task, session and message persistence and undermine the goal-parallel runtime. It remains a useful counterexample, not an implementation option.

The selected lower-contention design locks the already-existing `ProjectRuntimeAuthority.authorityPath` itself with the mature `fs-native-extensions` whole-file exclusive primitive: the marker is opened `r+`, and offset and length are both zero. Those exact arguments select Linux Open File Description locking, macOS `flock` and Windows `LockFileEx` without the rejected nonzero-range/read-descriptor incompatibilities. The locked descriptor is the identity read source; it must be a single-link regular file, remain the same filesystem object as the authority path, and contain a marker matching the current database UUID/path, project and worktree. No local snapshot lock file, database row, owner claim, lease file, stale timeout, repair or alias is introduced.

All in-repository authority mutation participates in that same ownership: existing-marker open/require reads, relocation and removal acquire the whole-file lock; relocation/removal fail explicitly if a publication owns it rather than replacing or unlinking the carrier. The asynchronous publication acquisition is abortable polling over `tryLock`, not a blocking event-loop wait. It also registers as an awaited Database lifecycle activity, so same-process close/reset/rebuild cannot delete or replace the database authority while a publication is active. The explicit project reset path and delete path must retain authority ownership through their destructive boundary; the global corrupt-database reset remains a separately confirmed destructive operation and cannot infer or recreate project authority.

Acceptance requires executable same-process and real-process contention, owner termination recovery, different-`OPENCORVUS_HOME` authority rejection, authority relocate/remove contention, lifecycle reset/close contention, Linux/macOS whole-file argument contract or native execution, and the existing parent/pointer/fault matrix. External same-user filesystem tampering is an integrity failure, not a supported second mutation path; every OpenCorvus mutation call point must nevertheless be covered. This design remains pending implementation and exact-tree review.

#### 2026-07-14 fixed project authority and destructive-lifecycle review correction

The first whole-file marker implementation exposed a deeper double-source defect before acceptance. `ProjectRuntimePaths.projectAuthorityPath` selected either the worktree-root marker or a Git-common-directory marker, and `Project.initGit` moved the marker only after `git init` made `.git` visible. No ordering can make that transition atomic for all processes: selecting the new path before rename creates a missing-authority window, while probing the old path when the new path is absent is a forbidden read fallback. Rename can also complete before descriptor cleanup fails, yielding a false operation failure after the identity already moved. The corrected single authority carrier is therefore always `<normalized-worktree>/.opencorvus.authority.json`, independent of Git state. Git common-directory identity still contributes to project-ID derivation, but never selects the authority pathname. `gitIdentityRoot`, `hasNonGitAuthority`, `relocateToGit`, dual-path enumeration and all relocation tests must be deleted; `git init` does not mutate authority identity.

The project marker cannot coordinate `Database.resetFiles` across all worktrees and processes. The database lifecycle therefore needs one separate, permanent, zero-byte, operating-system whole-file lock carrier derived only from the canonical `Database.Path()`. It contains no UUID, owner, claim, timestamp, lease, state or repair data and is not an authority or alternate database identity. Every process holds a shared whole-file lock on that carrier for the lifetime of its open SQLite connection. Database reset/rebuild first closes and releases its own shared connection lock, then must acquire the exclusive whole-file lock before opening, replacing or deleting SQLite files; a live connection in any process therefore prevents destructive replacement. SourceSnapshot does not acquire a second database lock: resolving the strict project marker opens the database and its caller-owned `Database.runLifecycleActivity` prevents the local shared connection from closing until publication settles, so a cross-process reset remains excluded for the complete publication. Shared connection locks preserve ordinary multi-process concurrency and per-project parallel hashing rather than serializing all commits behind a database-wide writer mutex. Lock contention fails explicitly, cleanup failure remains explicit, and no stale-file deletion or fallback path exists. The project marker remains the sole worktree/database/project identity source.

Caller-owned in-process `Database.runLifecycleActivity` remains necessary around the complete publication and project-deletion operation so same-process close/reset waits for asynchronous filesystem work. It must not be hidden inside the project-authority primitive because CLI reset enters the database reset lifecycle while holding the marker and cannot wait on itself. The CLI project reset holds the project marker, enters the database reset primitive (which owns the global database lifecycle lock), removes runtime targets, and removes the marker last. Global file-only reset does not enumerate or repair project markers; existing markers become explicit stale-authority conflicts against the newly created database identity.

The destructive-lifecycle call-point audit also found three unresolved platform bypasses that are recorded here and remain blocking debt after this authority slice. `ProjectGC.apply` automatically cascades project/session/task/memory rows after seven days without authority or active-execution evidence and must stop deleting user data. `ImplicitTaskProject.discard` removes the directory before a bare `Project.deleteRows` and must use the one explicit destruction primitive. Attachment reads and derived browser-thumbnail writes do not all acquire a strict project storage handle; a thumbnail can recreate `.derived` after project runtime deletion, while a GC cascade can delete a materialization lease before its asynchronous physical write settles. These paths require one strict Project-row-plus-authority storage-open contract and deletion participation; they must not be normalized as pre-existing harmless behavior.

The revised acceptance matrix adds: authority pathname invariance before/during/after `git init`; absence of every Git-marker/relocation symbol and artifact; shared database locks allowing concurrent processes while exclusive reset/rebuild is rejected until all other database connections close; SourceSnapshot activity retaining its process shared lock through publication; reset failure preserving the project marker; successful CLI project reset removing it last; database lifecycle lock cleanup diagnostics; and negative tests for the recorded GC, implicit-discard and derived-write bypasses before the overall project lifecycle can be accepted. This correction is pending implementation and exact-tree review.

#### 2026-07-14 exact-tree review rejection and lifecycle correction

The independent reviews returned `REJECT`; the preceding implementation checkpoint is execution history, not acceptance. Executable counterexamples found that a process can unlink the zero-byte database lifecycle carrier, recreate the same pathname, and acquire an exclusive lock on the new inode while another process still owns a shared lock on the old inode. Two lexical database paths that are filesystem links to the same physical SQLite file likewise derive two carrier paths and two lock domains. The repository does not currently reject a linked database path. The lifecycle protocol therefore must use one strict database identity before deriving the carrier, reject a database file or existing ancestor whose link topology permits a second lexical identity, and state the actual threat boundary: every participating OpenCorvus process and in-repository destructive operation is coordinated; an external same-user actor that deletes or replaces host-owned control files is unsupported integrity tampering and must be reported, not repaired. No filesystem carrier can remain a single kernel lock domain after a same-privilege external actor deliberately replaces its inode.

The reviews found additional lifecycle contract defects. `Database.rebuildSqlite` commits before restoring foreign keys, checkpointing, closing SQLite and releasing the lifecycle lock, but exposes every later error as an ordinary rebuild failure; its sole production caller, MySQL import, can therefore retry data that was already committed. `removeTargetsWithExclusiveLifecycle` loses `released_with_diagnostics` when target removal also failed. The primary connection reduces that cleanup state to a warning. `DatabaseLifecycleLock.release` must return a deeply immutable result at the primitive boundary, not rely on a reset wrapper. Every reset, rebuild, raw connection and primary connection caller must preserve operation error plus all cleanup evidence and distinguish `not_committed` from `committed_with_cleanup_failure`. SQLite close failure retains the live connection and shared lock for explicit retry.

The fixed project authority also remained visible as project source. `.opencorvus.authority.json` was absent from `ProjectRuntimePaths.isInternalRuntimeRelativePath`, `gitignoreEssentials`, the Git excluded-path list, workspace diff pathspecs, project/mission archive filtering, `ls` exclusions, expert-squad source enumeration, Architect/Build owned-path rejection and their prompts. A real `git add -A`, archive or source catalog can therefore capture its local database UUID and physical path, and a projected worker can edit it. The single root marker remains correct, but it is a host-owned root control path everywhere: Git status/index, archive/diff/enumeration, tool visibility, goal ownership and prompts must consume the one `ProjectRuntimePaths` constant. Tests must cover ordinary and force-tracked Git files; archive/diff filters are authoritative even when ignore rules were bypassed.

Initial marker publication also has a residue-order race: after `link(candidate, authority)` and before candidate unlink, a competitor scans candidate names first and reports a false integrity failure rather than opening and locking the published authority. Publication must lock the candidate descriptor before linking it, and existing-authority readers must lock the authority descriptor before evaluating candidate residue. A waiter that opened an old descriptor before authority unlink must never enter its callback; this executable negative is retained. SourceSnapshot acceptance adds a direct wrapper test: while publication is blocked inside its actual marker critical section, same-process `Database.resetFiles` or close cannot change DB files or pointer, then continues only after publication settles. Abort during real lock contention must release the descriptor and staging resources; a pre-aborted signal alone is insufficient.

The destructive-project audit expands the previously recorded debt into a blocking contract. `deleteCurrentProject` snapshots Task/Session owners before creating an Attachment-owned deletion row, physically deletes individual tasks before all owners settle, deletes config/rows before `Instance.dispose`, and ignores authority cleanup. The replacement is one project-owned destruction fact written first. Task, Session, all four TaskQueue enqueue paths, queue claim/new-loop, fresh dynamic dispatch, continuation, Attachment publication/read/thumbnail and every other durable project child must assert the absence of that fact in the same database transaction that creates new ownership. This is a data-integrity constraint, not a route preflight or workflow gate. Existing owners settle before any task row is physically removed; final destruction holds the project authority and database lifecycle, disposes the Instance before filesystem/database deletion, commits the project cascade once, removes the marker last, and reports committed cleanup failures explicitly. `ProjectGC.apply` may no longer delete user project rows. `ImplicitTaskProject.discard` must use the same explicit destruction owner. Bare `Project.deleteRows` production callers are removed. Permission, Memory, Cron, Event, Workspace, ControlTimeline, import/merge and delayed writers remain in the whole-repository inventory until each disposition is proven.

#### 2026-07-14 identity-bearing database lifecycle anchor revision

The independent native-lock design audit rejected the preceding zero-byte auto-created carrier. `fs-native-extensions` is advisory and binds the open filesystem object: Linux uses `F_OFD_SETLK`, macOS uses `flock`, and Windows uses `LockFileEx`. A directory lock, parent lock or ordinary empty lock file remains replaceable; locking the SQLite file itself conflicts with SQLite's own locking regions and still splits when reset unlinks the file; Windows named mutex is exclusive-only and would serialize all database processes. The accepted bounded threat model coordinates every participating OpenCorvus process, process death, path aliases, concurrent first start and every repository-owned destructive call. A same-privilege external actor that deliberately replaces a host-owned control inode and copies its valid identity, an administrator changing access controls/mounts, or a filesystem without documented native lock semantics is outside the guarantee and must never be described as protected.

The replacement is one `DatabaseLocation` physical-path abstraction plus one permanent identity-bearing lifecycle anchor. It resolves the nearest existing ancestor through native realpath, appends only the nonexistent suffix, rejects linked/reparse final database and carrier files, requires regular single-link files and provides the only database/carrier paths consumed by primary SQLite, raw SQLite, health, reset, CLI and scripts. No caller may independently use lexical `path.resolve(Database.Path())` as identity.

The carrier has strict content `{ schema_version: 1, lifecycle_uuid }`. `lifecycle_uuid` identifies the persistent lock domain across database generations; it is not a project identity, database-generation UUID, owner, lease, state or recovery instruction. The `database_identity` primary row binds the same required `lifecycle_uuid` to its fresh `database_uuid`. `DatabaseIdentity.currentUUID()` becomes a strict read and may not synthesize a row during ordinary access.

Provisioning is the sole carrier-creation path. When both database and carrier are absent, one contender creates the carrier with `wx+`, locks it exclusive, creates the schema and database identity, then atomically downgrades the native lock to shared before exposing the long-lived connection. When the database exists, a missing, malformed, replaced or multiply-linked carrier is an integrity error and is never recreated. A carrier without a database is the valid state immediately before first provisioning or after reset; the next primary open takes exclusive ownership, creates a new database generation UUID bound to the existing lifecycle UUID, then downgrades. Ordinary primary/raw opens acquire shared anchor ownership before SQLite open, verify the database binding while locked, close SQLite before releasing shared ownership and retain both on close failure. Reset/rebuild acquire exclusive ownership and never remove the anchor. Complete uninstall acquires exclusive ownership, deletes data, and removes the anchor last; `cli/cmd/uninstall.ts` is therefore part of this slice rather than an unrelated cleanup path.

`Database.rebuildSqlite` returns a typed commit result. Before `COMMIT`, failures are `not_committed` and preserve rollback/cleanup causes. After `COMMIT`, foreign-key restore, checkpoint, SQLite close or lifecycle cleanup failure is `committed_with_cleanup_failure`; MySQL import must not treat it as retryable non-commit. Reset target failure plus either `released_with_diagnostics` or `failed` cleanup preserves both cause graphs. Every primitive cleanup object and nested error list is frozen at its export boundary.

The final lifecycle matrix now includes two-process initial provisioning producing one lifecycle UUID/DB binding, missing carrier with existing DB leaving the filesystem unchanged, empty/random/symlink/hardlink replacement rejection, database symlink/hardlink and parent-alias convergence, reset preserving lifecycle UUID while changing database UUID, raw/primary close retry retention, reset/open and uninstall/open races, rebuild failures on both sides of commit, operation plus every cleanup state, Windows/Linux/macOS packaging/native smoke, and residue proof that direct SQLite opens and direct data-root deletion remain only inside the owned implementations. This revision supersedes the zero-byte-carrier paragraph above; that paragraph remains only as rejected design history.

#### 2026-07-14 lifecycle UUID over-abstraction correction

A second independent review rejected the proposed persisted `lifecycle_uuid` as unnecessary double identity under the threat boundary above. That correction is accepted before integration. Once all repository-owned processes use one physical `DatabaseLocation`, an existing database without its carrier fails without creating anything, reset/rebuild preserve the carrier, final database/carrier links are rejected, and uninstall owns exclusive lifecycle cleanup with carrier removal last, no supported internal operation can create the demonstrated second lock inode. A same-privilege external actor can copy a valid lifecycle UUID as easily as an empty carrier, so duplicating that UUID into both carrier and database does not extend the supported guarantee. It only expands schema, transfer and restore semantics.

The final design therefore retains a permanent strict zero-byte carrier, but removes every auto-create-on-existing-database path. Only the both-database-and-carrier-absent provisioning boundary may atomically publish and exclusively lock a new carrier. Carrier present plus database absent is the valid post-reset/unfinished-provisioning state and also requires exclusive initialization. Database present plus carrier absent is an integrity error. Ordinary existing-database open takes shared ownership and strictly requires an already persisted database-generation identity; it cannot lazily synthesize missing identity. Fresh provisioning creates the `database_identity` row while exclusive, then atomically downgrades the carrier lock to shared. This single generation identity remains the value bound into project authority. The acceptance matrix drops lifecycle-UUID round trips and instead proves stable carrier inode/path, fresh database UUID after reset, no missing-carrier creation, no direct uninstall deletion and no second persistent lifecycle identity in schema or carrier bytes.

#### 2026-07-14 Node sidecar lifecycle correction

The first real SourceSnapshot-backed Frontend Design visual test reproduced the same Browser Node sidecar failure twice: the second sequential render returned empty stdout, and Bun reported one dangling child process. The failure is below the product contract, so the test fixture must not hide it or retry it. `runBrowserNodeSidecar` currently resolves on the child `exit` event and immediately parses stdout; Node documents `close` as the event emitted after child stdio streams close. Parsing on `exit` can race the final stdout drain and leaves the stdio lifecycle open from Bun's perspective. The executor must settle successful and non-zero runs on `close`, retain `error`/abort/inactivity handling, and prove repeated sequential large JSON writes are fully drained without dangling children. This is a generic browser-sidecar lifecycle repair, not a Windows-specific product fallback. The original Frontend Design test command must pass unchanged afterward.

The `close` correction and its repeated-large-output test passed, but the original full Frontend Design file reproduced the dangling child a third time while the exact failing visual test passed alone. That narrows the direct trigger to the preceding page-error render. `StaticHtmlScreenshotScript` writes its result before browser cleanup and then suppresses every `browser.close()` failure. A failed or incomplete cleanup can therefore be reported as a successful terminal sidecar while its browser descendant survives into the next test. The script must compute the result, require browser cleanup, convert cleanup failure into the same visible failed result, and only write terminal JSON after cleanup completes. No cleanup error may be swallowed and no retry is permitted.

Reordering cleanup also passed its local contract but did not stop the full-file failure. Process inventory after the run showed no new surviving test Node/Chromium tree, so the remaining empty result is a child termination rather than a persistent descendant. The executor currently discards the child's exit code and signal when JSON parsing fails, collapsing termination into `invalid_json`. It must preserve that terminal evidence and classify invalid output from a non-zero or signaled child separately before any further root-cause claim.

#### 2026-07-14 database reset and existing-open root-cause Recall

The SourceSnapshot and goal-parallel suites are blocked by two database lifecycle defects, not by Frontend Design behavior and not by a Windows-only memory condition. Read-only independent review and a local executable counterexample established the causal chain:

1. The test preload creates only a temporary `OPENCORVUS_HOME`. `resetDatabase()` calls `Database.resetFiles()` before any database/carrier provisioning. `resetFiles()` currently calls `acquireExclusive()`, which correctly rejects a missing carrier, but this means the supported pristine destructive-reset boundary cannot initialize its permanent carrier.
2. After provisioning a real database/carrier, the first test and its reset complete. The next `Database.Client()` reaches a fresh lazy factory and `openOwnedSqlite`; this rules out a stale lazy cache. Existing-database open passes `{ create: false }` to Bun SQLite. A minimal process-local counterexample returns `SQLITE_MISUSE` for that constructor, while omitting the option opens and queries the same database successfully.

The single-source correction is:

- Add one explicit destructive-reset acquisition to `DatabaseLifecycleLock`: database present plus carrier absent remains an integrity error; carrier present takes exclusive ownership; database and carrier both absent atomically publish and exclusively own the permanent zero-byte carrier. Reset deletes only SQLite/WAL/SHM targets and retains the carrier.
- Replace the boolean SQLite open parameter with an explicit `create`/`existing` mode. Create mode passes `{ create: true }`; existing mode omits the option entirely. No `SQLITE_MISUSE` catch, retry or fallback is permitted.
- `Database.Client()` must reject a retained lifecycle-lock handle when no SQLite handle exists, rather than overwriting ownership after an incomplete cleanup.

Required tests cover pristine reset with retained carrier, database-without-carrier non-mutation, provision-close-existing reopen with a distinct connection, `resetDatabase()` followed by successful `Database.use`, cleanup failure retaining exact client/lock ownership, and real-process pristine reset/open contention. The production call-point inventory covers the sole `openOwnedSqlite`, primary open, reset/resetFiles, rebuild, `DatabaseLifecycleLock.acquireExclusive`, fixture preload and every reset fixture consumer. Existing carrier integrity and strict no-auto-create-on-existing-database tests remain authoritative.

#### 2026-07-14 generic task-artifact snapshot design correction

The first opaque TaskArtifactSnapshot proposal was independently `REJECT`ed because it retained workflow semantics from the old SourceSnapshot store. The corrected generic store has no current/latest pointer, parent snapshot, expected-parent compare-and-swap or child staging. Browser capture and Frontend Replica transformation are separate immutable publications connected only by explicit exact input ArtifactRefs recorded in the domain result. Selection/reuse is Orchestrator and EngineArtifact policy, never filesystem-store policy.

The minimum persistent manifest is strict `{schema_version, project_id, task_id, snapshot_id, trees}` plus its external manifest SHA-256 identity. Tree names are normalized opaque segments; each tree owns one exact sorted inventory of regular single-link files `{path,bytes,sha256}`. ArtifactRef binds the complete snapshot identity, opaque tree, normalized path, byte count and digest. The generic layer has no capture URL/viewport/action digest, reference image convention, source-package manifest, copies table, fixed tree enum or materializeSourcePackage. It does not return Blob copies for large trees.

Package publication is a task-only host capability injected into `ToolContext`; the host derives project ID, task ID and task runtime root from validated runtime authority. A package cannot supply those identities or an absolute destination. `begin` returns one opaque branded staging handle with host-created UUID and named tree directories below the task artifact root; `publish` accepts only that handle, builds and repeatedly verifies exact inventories, then commits under ProjectRuntimeAuthority exclusive ownership. Resolve/materialize returns a verified task-runtime path for cooperative filesystem consumption and revalidates before and after package execution. This is integrity/drift detection among participating OpenCorvus processes, not an untrusted-package sandbox: package tools already have `node:fs` and equal process privilege.

The correct runtime sequence is host browser capture -> generic capture snapshot publication -> existing `frontend-replica-source-researcher` consumes exact refs and publishes a separate derived snapshot -> Orchestrator persists both exact bindings and continues the normal dynamic-agent chain. The optional interface-modeler remains absent unless explicitly selected. EngineArtifact remains discovery/message evidence; a database-record failure after filesystem commit is reported as `snapshot committed, record failed` and cannot delete or relabel the committed snapshot.

Production cutover must be atomic: plugin ABI, host store, capture producer, source-researcher package transformer, exact-binding transports/consumers, runtime paths, manifest and payload land together while old SourceSnapshotStore, current pointer, duplicate package verifier, host compile/analyze and old registrations/tests are deleted. An idle second production publisher is itself a rule-8 violation. The following Frontend Design/Visual QA domain-schema migration remains a separate later cutover and cannot be conflated with this storage/producers slice.

#### 2026-07-14 headed E2E shutdown audit Recall

The independent shutdown audit returns `REJECT`. The first driver failure in the latest headed run was three EventSource `net::ERR_ABORTED` observations, not business inactivity and not a server-first shutdown: the isolated server was still returning successful requests and the implementer was still streaming. The page emits stream lifecycle synchronously, but the benchmark forwards it through an asynchronous page-to-Node binding and compares Node callback arrival sequence with Playwright `requestfailed`. That is a cross-channel race; a page-side closing can occur first while its Node callback arrives later. The report also omits raw lifecycle/classification rejection evidence, so unmatched transport failure cannot be distinguished after the fact.

The minimum generic correction is a synchronous page-realm ledger keyed by exact stream identity and URL. `requestfailed` consumes one already-recorded client-owned supersession from that ledger and retains the raw lifecycle/classification reason. An abort without one matching closing remains fatal. URL/`ERR_ABORTED` allowlists and cleanup-time suppression are forbidden.

`cleanupRealE2E` also owns the wrong order: it stops the server before closing the browser, then aborts execution, disposes instances and closes the database. This creates the later `ERR_CONNECTION_RESET` observations and makes the current cleanup unit test false-green because it asserts the wrong sequence. The required order is browser close while the server remains reachable, isolated server stop, live execution abort and settlement, registered Instance activity settlement, database post-commit effect idle, then database close.

Nineteen database-owner errors are not shutdown-only noise: seventeen bridge failures started while the build worker was active, before cleanup. The detached background build registers Instance activity but inherits a closed database effect owner; it must start through the existing `Database.runOutsideContext` boundary and then register activity. Message-bridge persistence and diagnostic failure writes must return awaited Promises to the Bus/effect owner rather than fire-and-forget work that recursively inherits the same closed owner. Windows process reclamation remains excluded by the user's instruction, but these database and asynchronous ownership defects are cross-platform product lifecycle issues and remain mandatory.

Shutdown acceptance requires real local SSE supersession and unmatched-abort negatives, raw classification evidence, browser-before-server cleanup proof, a background build started from a post-commit context with visible bridge writes and no closed-owner error, one observable diagnostic on injected persistence failure, activity/effect-idle ordering before database close, and a long-running semantic-activity test that exceeds historical wall-clock duration without timing out.

Authentication must be an explicit opaque task-scoped capture identity owned by the host. Agent inputs may reference that identity but may not read its credentials. #### 2026-07-14 SSE lifecycle accepted checkpoint

The page-sequence revision was independently rejected once more despite 35 green tests. A real production counterexample established an EventSource, destroyed the server response first, received Playwright `requestfailed`, then invoked the real handle's `close("superseded")` inside that Node callback. Because the page ledger created its failure observation only when later classification began, it incorrectly accepted the late closing. The active-close fixture was also false-green because it closed an already-settled stream rather than a live EventSource.

The accepted production contract adds a generic `failed` phase to the transport-protocol single source. Native EventSource publishes the exact stream's transport failure synchronously in the page realm before invoking business `onError`; a subsequent client `superseded` close cannot erase it. The ledger accepts only one exact opened -> closing lifecycle with the exact `superseded` initiator and no failed fact. Any transport failure, consumer close, wrong identity, duplicate consumption, malformed lifecycle or missing exact stream rejects. This is transport semantics, not a URL/error-text allowlist.

The final Node Playwright fixture loads a real Vite Overlay page and executes production `createTauriTransport("browser").openStream` and the real handle. It proves normal supersession is accepted after `close()` returns and the real request failure arrives; server destroy -> failed -> requestfailed callback -> late real superseded close remains rejected as `stream-has-transport-failure`; consumer/transport paths reject; duplicate and cross-ID consumption reject; and closing a BrowserContext with a live EventSource leaves `callbackCount === settledCount` and no pending classification. The browser harness closes the browser, awaits the page-close barrier and dynamically drains pending classifications, with no cleanup suppression or `setImmediate` snapshot.

Final independent exact-tree review returns scoped `ACCEPT`: 38 pass / 0 fail / 1285 assertions, real Node Playwright success, Transport Protocol/Overlay/OpenCorvus typechecks and scoped diff check. Combined with the preceding DB/cleanup checkpoint, lifecycle blockers are accepted. #### 2026-07-14 single-Page TaskArtifact capture design Recall

An independent producer-design review found that the old host pipeline has three network authorities, not one. `browser/webpage/extract.ts` creates and navigates one anonymous BrowserContext/Page before source actions; `browser/webpage/runtime-state.ts` creates and navigates a second anonymous BrowserContext/Page before applying actions; and the extractor downloads images again through Node `fetch`, outside both browser contexts. The sequential host pipeline then publishes pre-action HTML/DOM beside post-action reference/runtime evidence as if they described one page state. URL, viewport and action digests cannot prove that claim. `frontend-design/reference-capture.ts` is another independent capture sidecar with no current production caller.

The replacement host API is one generic `captureWebpageTaskArtifact` call. Its strict request includes project/task authority, source URL, explicit `{ kind: "anonymous" }` authorization, viewport and ordered actions. Authorization omission is invalid; raw cookies, headers, storage state, credentials and unknown fields are rejected. There is no viewport default, implicit action list, pipeline override, reuse/current/latest lookup or caller-supplied artifact identity. Authenticated capture remains a later explicit opaque task-authorization contract and is not approximated by inheriting a user browser profile.

One Browser, one fresh anonymous BrowserContext and one Page own the full capture. Before the sole `page.goto`, the sidecar installs response, request-failure, page-error and asset-body observation. It verifies zero inherited cookies, performs exactly one main navigation, rejects every main-document status of 400 or greater, waits for visible content and font readiness, executes the ordered actions with exact postcondition checks, and then captures HTML, extracted DOM/computed facts, reference pixels and initial runtime evidence from the same post-action page. Additional scroll/runtime screenshots remain on that Page. Browser response bodies and page-native data/canvas bytes are the only asset source; the Node image downloader is deleted. Browser and cleanup failures are aggregated and prevent publication.

The host writes one strict `capture` tree and a capture manifest containing the requested/final URL, explicit authorization kind, viewport, exact ordered actions, artifact roles/media types and complete inventory. Publication returns a strict BrowserCaptureBinding whose manifest, reference image and sorted artifact refs exactly equal the published tree inventory. Same-URL sequential and concurrent calls each create new snapshot identities. Missing, extra, cross-snapshot/tree, duplicate-path or digest-drift refs are invalid.

Implementation removes the independent extract/runtime-state sidecars and their Frontend Design wrapper registrations after their DOM/action helpers move into the single capture program. It also removes host compile/analyze/source-package stages, `url-data.json` and retry suggestions, swallowed network-idle probes and the unused reference-capture sidecar. WebClone parsing/IR generation does not move into this host API; it belongs only to the active source-researcher package tool.

Required tests use a real local HTTP server and Node-launched Playwright. A server that returns 403 once and 200 on a second request must still fail with an exact request count of one. Separate 401/403 cases preserve structured status and leave no published snapshot. A session-cookie fixture requires the same Context for action requests and protected assets, then proves action-state HTML/DOM/runtime/reference agreement. Schema negatives reject omitted authorization and secret-bearing fields. Browser/close failures discard staging. Source scans require one capture program with one `newContext`, one `newPage` and one `goto`, and zero production Node asset re-fetch, old wrapper tool IDs, retry/fallback text or current/parent paths. Sidecar progress is emitted during real browser work so the supervisor timeout remains semantic inactivity, not elapsed wall clock.

##### 2026-07-16 project-event subscription ordering review correction Recall

The first final-tree reviewer returned a concrete rejection before completing acceptance. ##### 2026-07-16 generic acceptance and requirement identity redesign Recall

The resumed goal first re-read this record, `specs/current/architecture/99-principles.md`, the complete AcceptanceSpec schema and execution call points, Goal schema/persistence/API surfaces, Requirements/Architect/Integrity adapters, requirement persistence/read projections, Workbench, Overlay, metrics, generated SDK/OpenAPI and their tests. The pushed General/SSE slice remains fixed at `363eada73a436a65b24a75d7617caf606dd08eb9`; the only pre-existing worktree change is the unrelated deletion of `dashboard/data/personas.json`, which remains excluded from this slice.

Three one-layer read-only audits independently rejected the current platform contract. They confirmed that `AcceptanceSpec.trigger` must be deleted rather than renamed: the per-goal evaluator was already removed, `on_integrity` has no dispatch or Integrity consumer, and the only remaining production reader reduces required contract audit behavior to essential severity. They also confirmed that `AcceptanceSpec.goal_id` duplicates its containing Goal and forces add-goal persistence to rewrite a second owner identity. Overlay demonstrates the resulting false contract by fabricating `source_requirement_id: "operator"` for an operator-authored criterion.

The accepted replacement is one strict generic source relation on the atomic acceptance spec:

```ts
source: {
  kind: string
  id: string
} | undefined
```

The object is strict and both values are trimmed nonempty strings. It is singular because an AcceptanceSpec is one atomic acceptance claim with one contract origin; a Goal aggregates multiple specs. It is optional because bootstrap, system and direct operator criteria can be valid without an upstream package-defined source. It is not a durable evidence ref: source identifies the contract origin, while evidence refs identify runtime proof. Generic Core does not interpret source kinds. The General Architect typed adapter requires `{ kind: "requirement", id: <known REQ-N> }` for every requirement-derived spec.

The first design draft proposed renaming `Goal.requirement_ids` to generic `source_refs`. A separate whole-tree audit rejected that as another dual source, and the original reviewer accepted the correction after a focused conflict review. There is no production use that cannot be derived from strict `goal.acceptance_specs[].source`: Build requirement context, Integrity status, Workbench status, acceptance coverage and requirement-to-goal traceability all derive the unique set of requirement sources on the Goal's local specs. Multiple Goals that implement the same requirement each own a local acceptance spec pointing to the same requirement. Therefore `Goal.requirement_ids` is deleted without a replacement field or cache. The Architect `register_traceability` tool, collector/result field and persisted/rendered traceability matrix are also deleted; any human-readable matrix is rendered on demand from the specs and is never an independently editable artifact.

Requirement storage retains two intentionally distinct identities without fallback: `engine_requirement.id` is the internal row primary key, while a new required `declared_id` is the adapter-declared logical identity. `(spec_snapshot_id, declared_id)` is unique. Requirements insertion validates the shared `RequirementDeclaredIDSchema`, snapshot copying preserves `declared_id` while generating a new internal row key, and every outward adapter/UI/matcher reads `declared_id`. `metadata.source_requirement_id`, `requestedID || requirementID`, `row.id` fallback and their positive legacy tests are deleted. The project is unpublished and database reset is the declared policy, so no migration or compatibility reader is added.

Malformed persisted data must fail at the read boundary. A shared acceptance parser performs JSON decoding followed by `AcceptanceSpecSchema.array().parse` with call-site context. Integrity requirement projection, Build contract audit, describe/render paths and other DB consumers stop casting, filtering malformed members or catching parse errors as empty arrays. Requirement acceptance, non-goals and evidence-ref readers likewise validate complete string arrays instead of silently filtering invalid members. `parseIntegrityAttemptPayload` is already strict and is not the source of the reported fallback; the defect is the empty-array recovery in `integrity/requirement-status.ts`.

Whole-tree call-point disposition is frozen as follows:

- generic schema and Goal ABI: replace `acceptance/types.ts`; remove `requirement_ids` from `pipeline/{goal-contract.schema,types}.ts`, `engine/{engine.sql,model,persist,store,describe}.ts`, `orchestrator/{goal-lifecycle-tools,build-tool,workload-analysis-tool,tools}.ts`, panel/task/workbench projections and generated SDK/OpenAPI;
- General typed adapters: add the shared declared-ID schema in Requirements, derive requirement coverage from spec sources in Architect/Build/Integrity, and remove `TraceabilityEntry`, `register_traceability`, collector/result/report persistence and the third model-authored mapping;
- requirement storage: add strict `declared_id` persistence/copy/read behavior and delete metadata identity/fallback in `engine/persist.ts`, `requirements/row.ts`, `integrity/requirement-status.ts`, `workbench/board.ts` and upstream catalog rendering;
- generic acceptance review: remove requirement coverage from the generic evidence manifest and project assessment, and remove `affectedRequirementIDs` from generic specialist findings instead of attaching every finding to every Goal requirement;
- metrics: `source_requirement_ids` has no production registration caller and is not allowed to preserve General terminology in a generic frozen-metric ABI; its dead source field is deleted while the still-used metric execution/result surface remains;
- Overlay: existing-goal edits send an owner-local AcceptanceSpec without fake source, goal ID or trigger; a real request-body regression is required;
- packages and fixtures: General, Mirror Watch and MirrorTest fixtures migrate destructively to the new source contract without aliases; package-specific REQ policy remains in the typed adapters/package prompts;
- generated and documentation surfaces: regenerate tracked OpenAPI, JavaScript SDK, schema snapshots and API docs, then run route/docs freshness and document-health checks.

Acceptance for this atomic slice requires: generic specs accept missing or custom structured source and reject every legacy field; General Architect rejects missing/non-requirement/invalid/unknown requirement source and derives exhaustive coverage; Goal roundtrip works without any requirement field; declared IDs are required, snapshot-local unique, copy-stable and never replaced by internal keys; malformed acceptance and requirement arrays throw; essential contract audit still blocks while nonessential audit remains advisory; Overlay emits no fabricated source; generic manifests and specialist reviews carry no requirement policy; and whole-tree negative scans find no production/test/generated `source_requirement_id`, `requirement_ids`, `register_traceability`, `on_goal`/`on_integrity` acceptance trigger or AcceptanceSpec `goal_id` residue. ##### 2026-07-16 strict installed-plugin failure semantics Recall

The original platform-runtime Goal and the complete Recall above were reread after the false plugin-tool surface was committed and pushed as `e9bb6004a0`. The branch and `myhexin/v0.0.7beta` are clean and equal at `e9bb6004a0047d5177d20ed915f4b629cd8d27cd`. The user requires fallback-free platform infrastructure and has explicitly placed all real E2E and headed GUI work last, so this slice changes only installed-plugin reliability contracts and their focused tests. No existing OpenCorvus or Overlay process is touched.

Whole-repository call-point scans cover `Plugin.init`, `Plugin.services`, `Plugin.list`, every `Plugin.trigger`, `runHookIsolated`, Config dependency preparation, `BunProc.install`, the dynamic plugin service route, Bus subscription/publish behavior, project-open lifecycle, EN/ZH plugin docs and all direct tests. A fresh one-layer independent read-only audit bound to the same clean HEAD returned `REJECT`: the installed-plugin interface still resolves partial capability sets after installation, import, factory, manifest, config, service or execution-hook failures.

The causal chain and disposition are fixed:

| Surface | Current defect | Required single semantics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Config local-plugin dependencies | Existing `package.json` read/parse errors become an empty object; failed `bun install` only warns; an unwritable directory is reported as not needing installation. | Create metadata only when genuinely absent, parse existing metadata strictly, reject failed installation, and reject when installation is required but the owned directory is not writable. `waitForDependencies` remains the truthful barrier. |
| Generic npm package cache | Corrupt cache metadata is replaced; missing/malformed installed version metadata can record the requested `latest` string. | Create cache metadata only on true absence and require a valid installed package version before persisting a resolved `latest` install. Provider and plugin callers share this strict package-install contract. |
| Internal/external plugin loading | Internal factory, module import, exported factory, manifest/schema/resource/backend and explicit npm install failures are caught, logged and skipped. A multi-export module can expose earlier hooks after a later export fails. | Reject Plugin state with phase/specifier context and original cause. Do not expose partial hooks or continue to later configured plugins. |
| Config and service registration | Config hook failures are swallowed. Service failures are stored as diagnostics, skipped and exposed only if a later request happens to use the matching manifest `serviceID`; `plugin.init` can report success with an invalid service registry. | Config and service factories are startup-required. `Plugin.init` runs strict config hooks and materializes the complete service registry; any failure or duplicate ownership rejects the `plugin.init` project-open stage. Preserve the named service-registration error as immediate context, remove deferred diagnostics lookup. |
| Mutating/execution hooks | `runHookIsolated` logs sync/async failure, returns `undefined`, continues later hooks and lets callers consume unmodified or partially mutated output. | Invoke in declared order and propagate the first failure with hook/specifier context to the owning LLM, command, shell, tool, compaction or message operation. Later hooks do not run and partial output is not consumed. |
| Event hook | The generic isolation wrapper erases failures before Bus can observe them. | Let the existing Bus subscriber aggregation reject `publish`; Bus already logs and propagates one failure or `AggregateError`. No second event-isolation mechanism is introduced. |
| Auth/provider callbacks | `Plugin.list` only returns successfully initialized hooks; callback consumers already await and propagate their own failures. | Retain their direct callback behavior. Strict startup loading prevents a partial list. |

The exact execution surface includes `chat.message`; LLM system/params/headers; message transform; compaction; text completion; command-before; shell environment for system terminal, shell execution and Bash; tool definitions; and tool before/after for native and package tools. `Plugin.list` consumers are CLI auth and provider auth/model loading. `Plugin.services` is owned only by the dynamic plugin route, while `Plugin.init` is owned only by project bootstrap. Declared SDK hooks `permission.ask`, `evaluation.checks`, `evaluation.result`, `evaluation.analysis` and `acceptance.ready` currently have no production trigger despite product documentation; this is separately recorded dead-contract debt and is not mixed into this failure-semantics correction.
